headline: Rain moves in Sunday afternoon and turns heavy at times Sunday night, around an inch in New York City, and a potentially larger coastal storm Wednesday night through Friday could bring heavy rain, strong winds and widespread coastal flooding over Thanksgiving.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Saturday is unusually warm and dry under high pressure: JFK reached 65 degrees by 2 PM, one short of its 66-degree record for the date, and Islip tied its record of 65. Tonight stays dry.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Low pressure moving up the coast brings some light rain as early as late morning or early afternoon Sunday, picking up late in the day and turning moderate to heavy at times Sunday evening; Sunday highs could again challenge records (Islip forecast 65 vs. a record 64). New York City should get about an inch, with 1–2 inches widespread across southern Connecticut and Long Island, locally near 3 inches in eastern Long Island and southeast Connecticut (where a few thunderstorms are possible Sunday evening), and about a half to three-quarters of an inch well north and west. East winds of 10–15 mph with gusts of 25–30 mph are possible along the coast Sunday night, with a low chance of brief 40–45 mph gusts out east if the storm tracks close enough. Rain ends by Monday morning as winds turn northwest to west, gusting around 15–25 mph; Tuesday looks dry.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Computer models continue to agree on a potentially large coastal storm from Wednesday night into Thanksgiving Day and Friday, likely more impactful than Sunday's, with heavy rain and strong east to northeast winds. Gusts could reach roughly 40–50 mph (35–45 knots) around the New York City airports on Thursday. The upper-air pattern is complex enough that small changes could shift the storm's strength, track and timing a lot.

coast: Coastal flooding with Sunday's storm looks minimal, since the biggest storm surge comes during the lower of the two high tides Sunday night; a few back-bay spots along the south shore of Nassau County could get close to minor flood levels Monday morning, but confidence is low. The Wednesday night–Friday storm is a bigger concern: high monthly tides mean many spots need less than a foot of surge to flood, and the current forecast supports widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding, possibly localized major flooding, plus beach flooding, erosion and overwash. On the water, Small Craft Advisories begin Sunday afternoon or evening and run to 6 AM Monday, with a Gale Watch Sunday evening through late Sunday night for the outer ocean waters and the nearshore ocean east of Moriches. Rough ocean seas linger into Monday night, then east-northeast winds ramp up Wednesday to gales Wednesday night and storm force on the ocean Thursday, with waves of 12–20 feet on the ocean (20–25 feet out east), 7–10 feet in Block Island Sound and 4–6 feet on Long Island Sound and at the entrance to New York Harbor.
watch_for: Sunday's storm track: a track farther west would mean more rain and wind for the city, farther east much less.
The Wednesday night–Friday coastal storm, which could bring widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding, heavy rain and strong winds over Thanksgiving travel.
Possible heavy downpours (up to 2 inches in 3 hours) in southeast Connecticut late Sunday evening.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in rain Sunday afternoon into Monday morning but less sure of the exact storm track and wind, and while models agree on a significant storm Wednesday night through Friday, its details are still uncertain.
